title: What Is Caching?
sources: AWS, 'What is Caching?' (aws.amazon.com/caching): a cache is a high-speed data storage layer that stores a subset of data, typically transient, so that future requests for that data are served faster than by accessing the data's primary storage location; caches are often kept in fast hardware such as RAM (in-memory)

Redis docs / glossary 'cache hit, cache miss': a cache hit is when requested data is found in the cache; a cache miss is when it is not, so the app reads from the database and usually stores the result in the cache (cache-aside pattern)
Redis docs, EXPIRE / TTL: a key can be given a time to live, after which it is automatically deleted, so cached data does not stay stale forever
Latency numbers every programmer should know (Jeff Dean / Peter Norvig, github gist jboner/2841832): reading from main memory is far faster than reading from disk or making a network round trip

lines.text: Yesterday we sent each order to the right chef,
lines.caps: *YESTERDAY | WE SENT EACH *ORDER | TO THE RIGHT *CHEF

lines.text: but what if everyone orders the same pizza?
Cooking it from scratch every time is slow.
So the kitchen keeps a few ready,
on a warm shelf right by the door.
lines.caps: ON A WARM *SHELF | RIGHT BY THE *DOOR

lines.text: When an order comes in, the waiter checks the shelf first.
lines.caps: WHEN AN *ORDER | COMES *IN | THE *WAITER | CHECKS THE *SHELF | *FIRST

lines.text: If it's there, that's a hit, served instantly.
so the chef cooks it and puts a copy on the shelf.
lines.caps: SO THE *CHEF | *COOKS IT | AND PUTS A *COPY | ON THE *SHELF

lines.text: Apps do the exact same thing:
they keep popular data in fast memory,
and skip the slow trip to the database.
so cached data gets an expiry timer.
